summary.text: A 25-year-old man with focal epilepsy after infant head trauma and hydrocephalus, controlled to seizures every 2-3 months on sodium valproate and oxcarbazepine, had psychiatric symptoms managed with olanzapine 2 years earlier. Ten days before admission valproate was switched to zonisamide, and 8 days later acute behavioral and emotional abnormalities emerged. The earlier symptoms had been alleviated with olanzapine; after the switch he also showed emotional instability, impulsiveness and unpredictable crying and laughing.

Admission diagnosis was epileptic psychosis. Mental examination showed angry affect, incongruence, infantile behavior, delusional speech and impulsive aggression without insight; PANSS 94 and BPRS 87. Electrolytes and toxicology screen were unremarkable; head CT is reported as showing brain atrophy in the case section and no significant abnormalities in the discussion (source conflict). Other tests were reported within normal limits and substance use was denied. Psychoactive-substance-induced disorder was in the differential and schizophrenia was not considered; the authors state the tests exclude infectious and metabolic causes and, citing the head CT, structural causes.

Initial therapy was zonisamide 200 mg/day, oxcarbazepine 0.6 g BID and olanzapine 10 mg BID. On day 2, with zonisamide-related psychosis suspected, zonisamide was stopped and sodium valproate sustained-release 1,500 mg/day was started with diazepam for agitation; olanzapine was reduced to 15 mg/day by day 6 for somnolence.

After discontinuation he gradually calmed, could answer simple questions by day 4, had no further seizures, and was discharged after 1 month with resolved symptoms; PANSS 7 and BPRS 5 are reported (no time stated in the text).

summary.text: A 48-year-old male police officer with post-traumatic epilepsy developed delirium and excessive suspicion lasting 15 years and was treated with zonisamide for at least 5 years. He was repeatedly hospitalized with a diagnosis of psychotic disorder due to trauma and epilepsy; epileptic psychosis and primary psychosis were excluded.

He had persistent command hallucinations, persecutory, erotic and noble-descent delusions and poor sleep, with PANSS 100 and BPRS 90. After he stopped zonisamide on his own for one week he had a generalized convulsive seizure; after zonisamide was resumed there were no more convulsions but he rambled all day with severe hallucinations and delusions.

Risperidone oral solution 4 ml/day was started with zonisamide continued, then increased to 6 ml/day with clozapine 150 mg/day added, without significant improvement; auditory hallucinations and delirious speech persisted. After six months of hospitalization he developed lower-limb weakness and general paralysis, forcing discharge and transfer for further treatment. Authors attribute the persistent psychotic symptoms to zonisamide.

caption_evidence.quote:
Fig. 3
Zonisamide inhibits the sustained high-frequency repetitive firing of action potentials dependent on Na^(+) and reduces the opening of T-type calcium channels, leading to the release of DA (dopamine) and 5-HT (serotonin). This excites nerve cells and stimulates the mesolimbic pathway, inducing and exacerbating psychiatric symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions/agitation, etc.

article_limitations: Figure pixels are inspected in the separate visual submission; figure-only values (e.g. Case 1 PANSS 81/BPRS 80 on day 3 and PANSS 20/BPRS 10 on day 6; Case 2 zonisamide 200 mg/day and 6-month discharge scores) are not in the text-based facts.
Case 1 head CT conflicts: brain atrophy (Case section) versus no significant abnormalities (Discussion); both kept review_only.
Case 2 psychotic symptoms are attributed both to trauma (diagnosis) and to zonisamide (Discussion); causal attribution remains the authors' judgment.
Case 2 self-stopping of zonisamide is one week in the text and 5 days in Figure 2.
Case 2 PANSS/BPRS have no stated time in the text; repeated after the narrative.

Discussion sentences about zonisamide pharmacology, approvals, off-label uses, doses above 100 mg/day and 2% psychosis incidence are literature/background and not assigned to either patient (cited references 1-10).
Case 1 consent statement mentions the subject and his parents; not assigned as a clinical fact.
Hospital and institution names appear in the source and are not extracted as facts.
Case 2 paragraph b00011 repeats the same treatment passage twice verbatim (editorial duplication); annotated once.
Case 1 discharge PANSS 7/BPRS 5 left untimed in text facts (adjacent-sentence time not borrowed); Figure 1 prints them under "Discharged".
